The Yellow-billed cuckoo (Coccyzus americanus) is a brood parasite host and obligate insectivore that breeds across much of the eastern United States. Newly hatched chicks emerge at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 8.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 8.5 grams], a value that reflects the species' relatively short incubation period. Eggs are incubated at an average temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], and under these conditions the total age at birth from the onset of incubation is 12 days [ab = 12 days]. This rapid embryonic development is characteristic of many Neotropical migrant cuckoos and contrasts sharply with the longer incubation periods observed in several non-parasitic members of the Cuculidae family. The newly emerged altricial nestling is entirely dependent on parental provisioning for thermoregulation and nutrition, and its initial body mass places it among the lighter cuckoo hatchlings documented in the literature. Subsequent growth during the nestling phase is rapid, driven by a high-protein diet of caterpillars and orthopterans.

Fledging represents a critical developmental milestone, occurring 21 days after hatching [tx = 21 days after hatching] under the typical thermal conditions experienced by active nestlings, which generally maintain a body temperature near 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. At this stage, the fledgling achieves its first flight and begins the transition toward independence from parental care. The post-fledging period is a particularly vulnerable phase, with mortality rates remaining elevated until the young bird becomes proficient at foraging and predator avoidance. Sexual maturation in this species is reached considerably later, with puberty estimated at approximately 63 days after hatching [tp = approximately 63 days after hatching] under the same active metabolic thermal regime at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. The onset of gonadal activity at this age marks the beginning of the juvenile's transition into a reproductively capable adult, though actual breeding is typically deferred until the following calendar year due to seasonal constraints on nesting opportunities.

The timing of first reproduction in Yellow-billed cuckoo is closely linked to its life-history strategy and migratory cycle. Individuals do not typically engage in their first brood until 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], a delay that corresponds to the return migration and territory establishment in the first spring following their birth year at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This reproductive milestone is achieved under active body temperatures of 41.3 °C, the same thermal regime at which fledging and puberty were observed. The first breeding event usually occurs in the second calendar year of life, meaning that birds hatched in early summer do not nest until the subsequent breeding season. This pattern is consistent with that seen in many other Neotropical migrant passerines and cuckoos that require a full year to acquire the necessary somatic and nutritional resources for successful reproduction. Females typically produce between 1 and 9 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 1 and 9 eggs per clutch], and they may complete approximately 1.5 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches annually] across the breeding season, with a typical peak in May through July.

Adult body mass is a key determinant of energetic demands and reproductive output in this species. The ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown females is approximately 62.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 62.5 grams], while males attain a slightly lower asymptotic mass of about 58.8 grams [Wwi = about 58.8 grams]. This modest degree of sexual size dimorphism is typical of Cuculidae and is likely related to the energetic costs of egg production and incubation in females. The initial wet weight of newly hatched chicks, which averages 9.1 grams [Ww0 = averages 9.1 grams], represents approximately 10.7 percent of the average adult female mass, indicating that a substantial proportion of somatic growth must occur during the nestling and fledgling stages. Growth rates during the first week post-hatching are particularly steep, with chicks doubling their emergence mass within just a few days. These rapid gains are supported by the high frequency of prey deliveries from both parents, who together may provision a single nest with dozens of large caterpillars per day during peak demand.

Longevity records for C. americanus from banding studies indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild is approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] under active thermal conditions near 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This value is relatively modest compared to that of larger, more slowly reproducing cuckoo species such as those in the genus Centropus, but it is consistent with the high annual adult mortality typical of small to medium-sized Neotropical migrants within the order Cuculiformes. Most mortality is concentrated in the first year of life, particularly during the post-fledging and first migration periods. Surviving adults face additional pressures from brood parasitism by Brown-headed Cowbirds (Molothrus ater), habitat fragmentation on both breeding and wintering grounds, and pesticide-induced reductions in their caterpillar prey base. The species' relatively short lifespan places a premium on early and repeated reproductive effort, which is reflected in its capacity to produce multiple clutches within a single season when conditions are favorable.
